“(i) Wide as they are, the powers of the Labour Court and the Industrial Court cannot extend to a direction to order 
regularisation, where such a direction would in the context of public employment offend the provisions contained 
in Article /4 of the Constitution; 


(ii) The statutory power of the Labour Court or Industrial Court to grant relief to workmen including the status of 
permanency continues to exist in circumstances where the employer has indulged in an unfair labour practice by not 
filling up permanent posts even though such posts are available and by continuing to employ workmen as temporary 
or daily wage employees despite their performing the same work as regular workmen on lower wages; 


(iii) The power to create permanent or sanctioned posts lies outside the judicial domain and where no posts are 
available, a direction to grant regularisation would be impermissible merely on the basis of the number of years of 
service; 


(iv) Where an employer has regularised similarly situated workmen either in a scheme or otherwise, it would be open 
to workmen who have been deprived of the same benefit at par with the workmen who have been regularised to make 
a complaint before the Labour or Industrial Court, since the deprivation of the benefit would amount to a violation of

Act, the employer should be engaging workmen as badlis, temporaries or casuals, and continuing them for years, with 
the object of depriving them of the benefits payable to permanent workmen.

“7. In contractual sphere as in all other State actions, the State and all its instrumentalities have to conform to Article

instrumentalities, with this element forming a necessary component of the decision making process in all State

arbitrariness. Rule of law does not completely eliminate discretion in the exercise of power, as it is unrealistic, but

Respondents, we see that while the learned single Judge was justified in setting aside the award af the Tribunal, the 
proper course to be adopted was to remit all the cases to the Tribunal. This we say for reasons more than one. Firstly,

length of officiation or discharge of duties and functions; quality of engagement, drawings, accounting of the post for 
each one of them, who have worked etc. All these issues will not be the same in all the cases. Therefore, each case

could have been granted without answering the individual issues; each issue relating to each case could not have 
been decided by the writ Court within the format of its adjudication procedures and scope. The adjudicating body, 
which has to do that activity, is the Industrial Tribunal. Therefore, we are of the view that while we would sustain the 
order of the learned singe Judge insofar as it interfered and sets aside the award of the Tribunal, the further findings 
and directions, issued through the impugned order have to go and the individual cases have to be sent back for 
consideration of the Tribunal. Such further procedure before the Tribunal will have to be carried forward with the 
materials already on record and also by affording an opportunity to the persons, who have claims as well as the 
management to place their rival contentions and further material before the Tribunal. The learned counsel appearing 
for the workmen are justified in pointing out that enormous delay has already happened and further action by the

The Tribunal thought that the question of the quantum of membership of the 2nd Respondent did not call for a finding

scanning the evidence given by the company and Respondent No. 3 to find out whether the terms of the settlement had 
been explained by the President of the union to the workmen or not and whether the workers voluntarily accepted the 
settlement knowing all the "consequences". This to our mind is again an entirely wrong approach. 


“When a recognised union negotiates with an employer the workers as individuals do not come into the picture. It is 
not necessary that each individual worker should know the implications of the settlement since a recognised union, 
which is expected to protect the legitimate interests of labour, enters into a settlement in the best interests of labour. 
This would be the normal rule. We cannot altogether rule out exceptional cases where there may be allegations of 
mala fides, fraud or even corruption or other induce- ments. Nothing of that kind has been suggested against the 
President of the 3rd Respondent in this case. That being the position, prima facie, this is a settlement in the course of 
collective bargaining and, therefore, is entitled to due weight and consideration. 


It is not possible to scan the settlement in bits and pieces and hold some parts good and acceptable and others bad. 
Unless it can be demonstrated that the objectionable portion is such that it completely outweighs all the other 
advantages gained the Court will be slow to hold a settle- ment as unfair and unjust. The settlement has to be 
accepted or rejected as a whole and we are unable to reject it as a whole as unfair or unjust. Even before this Court 
the 3rd Respondent representing admittedly the large majority of the workmen has stood by this settlement and that is

the appropriate Government by notification in the Official Gazette]. 


Compensation to workmen in case of transfer of undertakings. 
Section 25B defines the term continuous service which provides 
Definition of continuous service.- For the purposes of this Chapter, -- 


() a Workman shall be said to be in continuous service for a period if he is, for that period, in uninterrupted service, 
including service which may be interrupted on account of sickness or authorized leave or an accident or a strike 
which is not illegal, or a lock- out or a cessation of work which is not due to any fault on the part of the Workman; 


(2) where a Workman is not in continuous service within the meaning of clause (7) for a period of one year or six 
months, he shall be deemed to be in continuous service under an employer-- 


(a) for a period of one year, if the Workman, during a period of twelve calendar months preceding the date with

(i) one hundred and ninety days in the case of a Workman employed below ground in a mine; and

Ltd case, held as under: 


"These changes brought about by Act 36 of /964 appear to be clearly designed to provide that a Workman who has 
actually worked under the employer for not less than 240 days during a period of twelve months shall be deemed to 
have been in continuous service for a period of one year whether or not he has in fact been in such continuous service 
for a period of one year. It is enough that he has worked for 240 days in a period of /2 months, it is not necessary that 
he should have been in the service of the employer for one whole year." 


In a concurring judgment Pathak J. agreed with this interpretation of section 25B(2). Therefore, both on principle and 
on precedent it must be held that section 25B(2) comprehends a situation where a Workman is not in employment for 
a period of 72 calendar months, but has rendered service for a period of 240 days within the period of /2 calendar 
months commencing and counting backwards from the relevant date, i.e. the date of retrenchment. If he has, he would 
be deemed to be in continuous service for a period of one year for the purpose of section 25B and 
Chapter VA.”

upon the Workman to show that he has completed 240 days of the service with the Respondent just preceding from 
the date of his termination. Further, in respect of the employment of calculating the 240 days service in view of the 
contents of Section 25-F read with Section 25-B of the I.D. Act, 947.

“(i) Wide as they are, the powers of the Labour Court and the Industrial Court cannot extend to a direction to order

(ii) The statutory power of the Labour Court or Industrial Court to grant relief to workmen including the status of 
permanency continues to exist in circumstances where the employer has indulged in an unfair labour practice by not 
filling up permanent posts even though such posts are available and by continuing to employ workmen as temporary 
or daily wage employees despite their performing the same work as regular workmen on lower wages; 


(iii) The power to create permanent or sanctioned posts lies outside the judicial domain and where no posts are 
available, a direction to grant regularisation would be impermissible merely on the basis of the number of years of 
service; 


(iv) Where an employer has regularised similarly situated workmen either in a scheme or otherwise, it would be open 
to workmen who have been deprived of the same benefit at par with the workmen who have been regularised to make 
a complaint before the Labour or Industrial Court, since the deprivation of the benefit would amount to a violation of 
Article /4, and 


(v) In order to constitute an unfair labour practice under Section 2(ra) read with Item /09 of the Vth Schedule of the ID 
Act, the employer should be engaging workmen as badlis, temporaries or casuals, and continuing them for years, with 
the object of depriving them of the benefits payable to permanent workmen.

“7. In contractual sphere as in all other State actions, the State and all its instrumentalities have to conform to Article 
34 of the Constitution of which non-arbitrariness is a significant facet. There is no unfettered discretion in public law: 
A public authority possesses powers only to use them for public good. This impose the duty to act fairly and to adopt a 
procedure which is ‘fairplay in action’. Due observance of this obligation as a part of good administration raises a 
reasonable or legitimate expectation in every citizen to be treated fairly in his interaction with the State and its 
instrumentalities, with this element forming a necessary component of the decision-making process in all State 
actions. To satisfy this requirement of non- arbitrariness in a State action, it is, therefore, necessary to consider and 
give due weight to the reasonable or legitimate expectations of the persons likely lo be affected by the decision or else

fides of the decision in a given case. The decision so made would be exposed to challenge on the ground of 
arbitrariness. Rule of law does not completely eliminate discretion in the exercise of power, as it is unrealistic, but

dependant employment scheme and he discharged his duties to the utmost satisfaction of his superiors without any 
kind of adverse remarks. While he was working under the control of the Respondent No.l, due to underground 
atmosphere and coal dust, he suffered from severe Typhoid and ill-health and unable to attend to his duties regularly. 
Further, he sustained injuries to his knees and was compelled to undergo prolonged treatment in the Govt. Hospital, 
Karimnagar. But, the Respondent No.| issued charge sheet dt.Il..997 to him alleging that the petitioner absented 
to duties from January to September 997:- 


“25.25: Habitual late attendance or habitual absence from duty without sufficient cause from 
January 997 to September 79977

hard ship and misery to eke out lively hood for all his family members. The limitation of 3 years was brought into 
force as per the Amendment Act 200 and the petitioner was dismissed from service prior to the said Amendment Act.

jurisdiction of this Tribunal are not sustainable under Law. 


0(a). Further, with regard to the contention of delay and barred by limitation, this Tribunal relied on a D.B. Judgment 
of the Hon’ble Supreme Court in Civil Appeal No.257/999, dt.08.04.999 between Ajaib singh vs. Sirhind Co-op. 
Marketing-cum-Processing Service Society Ltd., & another, wherein their lordships held that:- 


“Article ॥37 of schedule of Limitation Act not applicable to the proceedings under ID. Act. The object of Industria 

give succor to weaker sections of the society. The emergence of the concept of Welfare State implies an end to exploitati 
a corollary to that collective bargaining came into it own. The Legislature had intended to protect workmen againsi 
exploitation by the employer and to ensure termination of Industrial Disputes in a peaceful manne) 


The object of the Act, therefore, is to give succor to weaker sections of the society which is a pre-requisite for Wel, 
industrial peace and pre-empt industrial tension, the Act further aims at enhancing the industrial production which is ac 
blood of a developing society. 


The Act provides a machinery for investigation and settlement of industrial dispute ignoring the legal technicalities 
delays, by specially authorized Courts which are not supposed to deny the relief on account of the procedural 


0(b). Further, relied on a decision of the Hon’ble High Court reported in 20I2 (l) ALD 220 (DB), wherein their 
lordships held that:- 


“The Industrial Disputes Act, 94778 a social welfare legislation, which required to be interpreted keeping in view t 
Preamble and Directive principles of State Policy in Part-IV of the Constitution. Merely because workman approached 
delay, relief cannot be denied. No indication in the Act that delay extinguishes right conferred on the workmen under 
Labour Court is conferred with very wide discretion ७/४९९77-१ from considering the delay on part of workmen in 


Section 2-4 (2) or Section 700) of the Act do not prescribe any period of limitation for raising industrial dispute. 

Limitation Act, /963 has no application (Ajaib Singh’s case supra). Merely because the workmen approached the Inc 

delay, the relief cannot be denied. The Act nowhere gives an indication that the delay extinguishes the right conferred o 

Industrial Law. The Industrial Court conferred with very wide discretion 9/5९८,.77-4 of the Act, is not precluded from ¢ 
on the part of workman in granting relief”. 


0(c). Further, the Hon’ble Gujarath High Court following the Hon’ble Supreme Court, in a judgment dt.l5.02.2020 
Between: Dharampur Nagarpalika Vs. Mahendrasinh Narsinh Padhiyar their Lordship have observed that: - 


(a) Law of limitation does not apply to the proceedings under the Industrial Disputes Act, /947. 


(b) The words ‘at any time' used in Section 79 would support that there is no period of limitation in making an 
order of reference. 


(c) At the same time, the appropriate Government has to keep in mind as to whether the dispute is still existing 
or live dispute and has not become a stale claim and if that is so, the reference can be refused. 


(d) Whether dispute is alive or it has become stale/non-existent at the time when the workman approaches the 
appropriate Government is an aspect which would depend upon the facts and circumstances of each case 
and there cannot be any hard and fast rule regarding the time for making the order of reference. 


Their Lordships have further held that: This Court shall need to regard, of course, the later decision which 
speaks of grant of back wages as if he was not illegally terminated. However, the period for which there is no 
initiative taken by him from the year 995 to 2097, the same will have to be treated as dias-non. It is also not 
possible for a driver not to be working for all these years with his skill as a Driver and therefore, according 
to this Court, (/५८4/2404/2077 JUDGMENT the back wages shall have to be reduced to 80% from the date 
of filing of the reference as dias-non. 


l0(d). Apart from the above, their Lordships of the Division Bench of Hon’ble Rajasthan High Court in a recent 
decision Between: Heera Ram Vs. Assistant Engineer, Irrigation and others, dt.08.02.2023, wherein their lordships 
held that:- 


...Law can be summarized that there is no prescribed time limit for the appropriate Government to exercise 
its powers under Section 79 of the Act. It is more so in view of the language used, namely, if any industrial 
dispute exists or is apprehended, the appropriate government “at any time” refer the dispute to a Board or 
Court for enquiry. The reference sought for by the workman cannot be said to be delayed or suffering from a 
lapse when law does not prescribe any period of limitation for raising a dispute under Section 79 of the Act. 
The real test for making a reference is whether at the time of the reference, dispute exists or not and when it is 
made it is presumed that the State Government is satisfied with the ingredients of the provision, hence, the 
Labour Court cannot go behind the reference. It is not open to the Government to go into the merit of the 
dispute concerned and once it is found that an industrial dispute exists then it is incumbent on the part of the 
Government to make reference. ... we do not think that the delay in the case on hand has been so culpable as

to disentitle him any relief. We are also satisfied that in view of the details furnished and explanation offered, 
the workman cannot be blamed for the delay and he was all along hoping that one day his grievance would be 
considered by the Management or by the State Government.” 


0(e). It is not in dispute that in the present case on hand, the petitioner was dismissed from service by the Respondent 
No.2/ General Manager vide Ref. dt.24/26.04.998. The learned counsel for the petitioner strenuously contended that 
the petitioner moved before the respondents for 7-years through union leaders. After moving from pillar to post, he 
lost all his hopes approached this Tribunal and filed the I.D. petition on 29.0.205. But, it was returned on the Bench 
by docket order dt.0l.08.209 and later on re-submission on 03.07.2025, this Tribunal registered the same on 
4.07.2025. Thus, there is continuation of cause of action and the dispute is alive. For about 6-years from 999 to 
205, the petitioner kept quiet and he raised the dispute before this Tribunal during 205. Hence, there is no abnormal 
delay on the part of the petitioner, the dispute cannot be said to be stale or non-existent and the dispute is alive and 
deserves to be adjudicated by this Tribunal judiciously. 


l. Therefore, in view of the above cited decisions and facts and circumstances of the present case on hand, I am of 
the considered view that there is no force in the contention of the learned counsel for Respondents/Company with 
regard to delay. Further, it is a fact the whole ILD. (Amendment) Act, 200 was repealed by the Central Government 
vide the Gazette of India dated 097 May 206 and limitation period is not applicable to the provisions of Industrial 
Disputes Act. But, this Tribunal has to mould the relief by considering the facts and circumstances of each case. 
Hence, the doubts raised by the learned counsel for the respondents are like that of a “Doubting Thomas”, 
which are not real and tangible doubts. Accordingly, it is answered in favour of the petitioner and against the 
respondents’ Singareni Collieries Company Limited. 


2. Further in this matter, initially the petitioner/workman denied the validity and legality of the enquiry report. 
But on 20.0.2026, the learned counsel for petitioner filed Memo U/Sec.-A of I.D Act by accepting the procedure 
of domestic enquiry to be fair and valid. Hence, it can be said the Enquiry Officer has followed the principles of 
natural justice. Now the next question is, whether the misconduct is proved in the facts of the case and the findings are 
not perverse. So, this Tribunal is to re-appreciate the evidence and come to its own conclusion with regard to finding 
guilty or not based on evidence. Accordingly, the Point No.| is answered. 


POINT No.2 & 3: 


3. In view of the pleadings of the Petitioner/Workman as well as Respondents/corporation as well as in view of the 
rival arguments of their respective counsel now this Court will go into the evidence on record. Admittedly, the 
petitioner was dismissed from service by Ref. dt.24/26.04.998 wherein it is alleged that the petitioner was absent 
from duty without sanctioned leave or sufficient cause during the year 997 i.e., for 9-months from January 997 to 
September 997. From a perusal of the record, it shows that Charge Sheet dt.l..997 was issued to the petitioner. 
It is evident from the domestic enquiry proceedings dt.03.02.998 and enquiry report 04.02.998 under Ex.M-! and 
Ex.M-2 that the petitioner absented to duties for 9-months from January 997 to September, !997. Further, a perusal 
of these documents under Ex.M-| and Ex.M-2 would goes to show that the Petitioner participated in the domestic 
enquiry and deposed that he remained absent on the dates as mentioned in the charge sheet and it was his mistake. He 
admitted the charges framed against him and pleaded guilty and deposed that due to Jaundice and Typhoid, he could 
not attend for his duties during the year 997. He further admitted that he did not inform the Management in advance 
about his absence. 


3(a). From the Enquiry Report which is also under Ex.M-2, it is further evident that the petitioner absented to duty 
without sanctioned leave and he accepted the charge made under Company’s standing order 25.25 (Habitual late 
attendance or habitual absence from duty without sufficient cause) mentioned in the charge sheet dt...997 was 
held proved. It appears that the petitioner submitted medical certificate from 07.07.997 to 24.0.998, which shows 
that he did not attend to his duties from January 997 to 24.0.998. The charge sheet period is January to September 
997, but beyond that period, the petitioner remained absent till 24.0!.!998. Further vide letter dt.9/20.03.998, the 
petitioner was given another opportunity to submit representation on the enquiry findings report within 7 days. The 
dismissal order dt.24/26.04.!998 is marked as Ex.M-4 wherein it shows that considering the charge leveled and 
proved against the petitioner being grave and serious, he was dismissed from services of Company w.e.f., 30.04.998. 


3(b). It is clear that the petitioner has not attended to duties during the charge sheet period and the charges were 
amply proved against him. Therefore, it can be said that the respondents/ company has no axe to grind against the 
petitioner. Hence, this Tribunal has no hesitation to hold that the charge leveled against the petitioner/ workman is 
proved and misconduct of the workman is established basing on the evidence and the findings of enquiry officer are 
not perverse. 


4. Now the question is whether the punishment of removal from service is disproportionate or not? 


4(a). It is settled law that the object of I.D.Act is to give succor to weaker sections of the society and it is a social 
welfare legislation. Here, there is no “Plumbline Precision” for deciding the proportionality of punishment, which 
depends upon the facts and circumstances of each case. The Industrial Tribunal/Labour Court is empowered to 


538 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA : MARCH |4, 2026/PHALGUNA 23, 947 [PART II—SEc. 3(ii)] 


exercise discretionary powers U/Sec.ll-A of Industrial Disputes Act for judicious adjudication of the industrial 
disputes. Several factors like nature of duty, past service past conduct, previous penalties if any and the discipline 
required to maintain in the department, victimization and plea of the petitioner/workman and the punishment must be 
commensurate with the gravity of charge against the petitioner/workman etc., by considering the relevant factors and 
mitigating circumstances of each case are to be taken into consideration so as to mould the relief appropriately and 
reduce the punishment imposed on the petitioner/workman. 


5. Here, the learned counsel for the petitioner/workman submitted that the Petitioner was appointed in the year 205 
and rendered very short service of about 2-years. Wide powers are vested in Labour Court or Tribunal. Labour Court 
can temper justice with mercy and give an opportunity to an erring workman to reform himself. The petitioner 
remained unemployed from the date of dismissal, he hails from a very poor family, he has got no other livelihood and 
facing untold financial problems, and prayed to consider the case U/Sec.ll-A of I.D. Act., by granting another 
opportunity to serve the Company. 


6. Here, this Tribunal relied on a Division Bench Judgment of the Hon’ble Supreme Court rendered in Civil Appeal 
No.257/999, dt.08.04.999 between Ajaib Singh vs. Sirhind Co-op. Marketing-cum-Processing Service Society 
Ltd., & another, wherein their lordships held that:- 


“The object of Industrial Disputes Act was to give succor to weaker sections of the society. The emergence of the 
concept of Welfare State implies an end to exploitation of workman and as a corollary to that collective bargaining 
came into it own. The Legislature had intended to protect workmen against victimization and exploitation by the 
employer and to ensure termination of Industrial Disputes in a peaceful manner. 


“The object of the Act, therefore, is to give succor to weaker sections of the society which is a pre-requisite for 
Welfare State. To ensure industrial peace and pre-empt industrial tension, the Act further aims at enhancing the 
industrial production which is acknowledged to be life-blood of a developing society. The Act provides a machinery 
for investigation and settlement of industrial dispute ignoring the legal technicalities with a view to avoid delays, by 
specially authorized Courts which are not supposed to deny the relief on account of the procedural wrangles”. 


l6(a). Further, in a decision of the Hon’ble High Court reported in 20I2 (.) ALD 220 (DB), wherein their lordships 
observed that:- 


“The Industrial Disputes Act, /947 is a social welfare legislation, which required to be interpreted keeping 
in view the goals set out in the Preamble and Directive principles of State Policy in Part-IV of the Constitution. 
The Labour Court/Industrial Tribunal is conferred with very wide discretion 9/8९८77-4 of the Act for granting 
appropriate relief”. 


7. Here, their Lordships of the Hon’ble Gujarat High Court in a case rendered on 04.05.994, Between: Management 
of Glaxo India Ltd., Vs. State of Assam and 3 others categorically observed that “a Labour Court is required to settle 
a dispute according to the principles of natural justice, equity and good conscience and law without attaching 
undue importance to legal technicalities”. 


8. Further, it is well settled law that if the Industrial Tribunal/ Labour Court is satisfied that the punishment imposed 
on the petitioner/workman is not justified, the Industrial Tribunal/ Labour Court is clothed with the power to 
reappraise the evidence in the domestic enquiry and satisfy itself whether the said evidence relied on by the Enquiry 
Officer or Respondents/ Management established the misconduct alleged against the workman. Further, 3९८7-१4 
comes into effect only at the time when the Industrial Tribunal/Labour Court considers about the punishment to be 
imposed. While previously the Industrial Tribunal/Labour Court had no power to interfere with the punishment, it is 
now clothed with such a power. Apart from the above, Industrial Tribunal/Labour Court should temper justice with 
mercy and not flog the petitioner/ workman to asset our might. The power of ocean does not lie in its tumultuous tides 
but in its meditative vastness”. My above view is fortified with the observation of their Lordships of Hon’ble Madras 
High Court in a case Between: High Court of Madras Vs. R.D.Santhana Krishnan बॉ. 2477 December, 2024. 


9. Here, it is to be noted that the concept of Industrial Dispute is quite broad and with the passage of time its horizon 
is being expanded. Further, the disputes are required to be resolved for the purpose of establishing peaceful and 
cordial atmosphere in an industry. Peace and harmony are the quintessential aspects which are to be kept in view 
while dealing with the “/is” or “controversy” relating to any industry. Apart from the above, whether the impugned 
punishment is so disproportionate as to shock the conscience of the Court, has to be decided on the facts of each case, 
having due regard to the gravity of misconduct & nature of duties discharged by the delinquent employee. 


20. Here, it is pertinent to note that the term “misconduct” is the intentional doing of something which the doer knows 
to be wrong, or which he does recklessly, not caring what the result may be. It includes negligence or want of proper 
care which an employee is to take. But, it is a fact that “to err is human” and “to forgive is divine”. Keeping the said 
spirit into consideration and in the interest of cause of justice, every errant conduct of an employee of an organization 
could not be treated as grave misconduct. Further, it is settled law that promoting empathy and understanding by 
encouraging forgiveness, which is a divine quality transcending human limitation, should be preferred to anything else 
in the given circumstances. My above view is fortified by observation of their Lordships of the Hon’ble Supreme 


[भाग I—aves 3(ii)] भारत का राजपत्र : मार्च 4, 2026/फाल्गुन 23, 947 539 


Court in a judgment rendered Between: Ratilal Jhaverbhai Parmar Vs State Of Gujarat 4.27 October, 2024. 


2. Further, the Hon’ble Madras High Court observed in a case rendered in Management of Hyudai Motor India Ltd 
Vs. T.Sudhakar ... on 377 January, 2022: 


“When scales of justice stands balanced in a given case, the tilt to be exercised should be in favour 
of the poor workmen rather than the mighty Managements.” 


22. Here, I am of the opinion that for promoting ethical behavior and integrity for Public Servants, the Latin Maxim 
(Memento Mori: remember that you must die”) acts as a check against selfish to selfless service. It serves as a 
reminder that: “when office is gone, only the legacy of their character remains”. So, the old Adam or old Man or old- 
self of him or her must die. Otherwise, it will kill them. In summary, Memento Mori serves as a sobering, yet 
empowering reminder that allows Public Servants to focus on leaving a positive, lasting impact rather than chasing, 
selfish and temporary goals. 


23. Therefore, by taking a holistic view of the matter, I am of the considered view that the extreme punishment of 
dismissal from service imposed by the respondents/company against the petitioner/workman is harsh, disproportionate 
and shocks to conscience of this Tribunal, hence, deserves to be modified since the disciplinary authority cannot be 
permitted to act arbitrarily and work like a Roman Knight and it cannot be allowed a fight between David and Goliath 
as in the present case on hand. Moreover, facts of this case attracts the proverbial saying “Every saint has a past and 
every sinner has a future” and Biblical proverbs “Speak up for those who cannot speak for themselves, for the rights 
of all who are destitute” and “Speak up and judge fairly; defend the rights of the poor and needy.” Further, “Heavens 
would not have fallen if one more opportunity is given for the petitioner”. 


24. This Tribunal has perused, analyzed and meditated upon the case at hand, the case laws and principles of law 
referred above. In view of the above facts and circumstances and keeping in view of the principle “temper justice with 
mercy” and to meet the ends of justice, this Tribunal is of the opinion that the punishment of removal from service 
imposed on the petitioner is disproportionate and shocks the conscience of this Tribunal and hence, it deserves to be 
modified appropriately. It appears from the record that the petitioner rendered very short service of less than 2-years in 
the respondents’ company and he is out of employment ever since his dismissal from service. Hence, this Tribunal is 
of the considered view that that the petitioner/workman deserves to be reinstated into service as “AFRESH BADLI 
FILLER” only. The petitioner is not entitled to any back wages, continuity of service and any other attendant benefits. 
Hence, the punishment of dismissal from service imposed by the Respondents’ Company is hereby modified. 
Accordingly, the Points 2 & 3 are answered. 


25. IN THE RESULT, the petition is partly allowed. The dismissal order dt.24/26-04-998 under Ex.M-4 issued by 
the Respondent No.2 is hereby modified. The respondents’ company is directed to reinstate the petitioner into service 
as “AFRESH BADLI FILLER” only. The petitioner is not entitled to any back wages, continuity of service and any 
other attendant benefits. However, the petitioner is entitled to the salary only from the date of publication of the 
Award. Copy of the Award be sent to the appropriate Government for publication. Both parties shall bear their own 
costs.

This case coming before me for final hearing in the presence of Sri Javvaji Srinivas, Advocate for the 
Petitioner and of Sri T. Ravinder Singh, Advocate for the Respondents; and having been heard and having stood over 
for consideration till this day, the Tribunal delivered the following: 


-: AWARD :- 


This is a petition filed U/Sec.2-A (2) of I.D. Act, 947 praying to set aside the dismissal order dt.I8.05.209 
issued by Respondent No.2 and to direct the respondents’-company to reinstate the petitioner into service with 
continuity of service, all other consequential attendant benefits and full back wages. 


2. The alpha and omega of the case of the petitioner is as follows:- 


2(a). | The petitioner was appointed in the respondents’ company during the year 20I5 as Badli Worker and he 
discharged his duties to the utmost satisfaction of his superiors without any kind of adverse remarks. His mother 
Kanapaka Kamala Bahi was suffering from chronic ill-health and he imparted prolonged treatment to her at MGM 
Hospital, Regional Eye Hospital, Warangal and other hospitals. He is the only person to look after his mother and he 
faced severe financial crisis in connection with amounts payable to his sisters. He suffered from mental distress and 
ill-health, due to which he could not attend to his duties regularly and put-in (5) musters during the year 20l6. As he 
continued to work in the underground on one hand and was imparting treatment frequently to his ailing mother and for 
himself on the other hand. But, the Respondent No.2 issued charge sheet dt.l8.02.20l7 to him alleging absentee 
during the year 206:- 


“25.25: Habitual late attendance or habitual absence from duty without sufficient cause”’. 
“25.3l: Absence from duty without sanctioned leave or sufficient cause or overstaying beyond sanctioned leave”. 


2(b). The petitioner submitted satisfactory explanation and participated in the domestic enquiry conducted on 
6.09.20!7. There is no deliberate absenteeism on his part and there is reasonable and sufficient cause for not 
attending to his duties during the charge sheet period of 20l6. He improved his attendance during the years 20l7 and 
208 and his performance during the above years is furnished here under:- 


The respondent No.| served charge sheet and obtained written explanation from him, assuring that he will be allowed 
to duty. He participated in the enquiry proceedings on !6.09.20I7, deposed the true facts of ill-health of his mother, 
himself and his family problems. But, the enquiry officer did not properly appreciate the documentary and oral 
evidence, his findings are very cryptic and he gave his vague findings, which are quite biased and perverse. The 
Respondent No.2 required him to make representation on the findings report of the Enquiry Officer by letter 
dt.0.02.208, to which he submitted his satisfactory explanation on 3.02.208. But, the Respondent No.2 unjustly 
dismissed him from service by Ref. dt.l8.05.209 with effect from 27.05.20I9 straight away, without issuing any 
prior Show Cause Notice proposing the said capital punishment of dismissal from service. 


2(c). | The petitioner preferred Appeal and moved from pillar to post before the respondents. After more than (02) 
years, Respondent No.3 rejected his appeal vide Ref. dt.6.07.202. Having lost his hopes, the petitioner approached 
this Court seeking justice. There is sufficient and reasonable cause for the petitioner for not attending to duties during 
the charge sheet period. As such, it cannot be termed as serious misconduct warranting the extreme punishment of 
dismissal from service. Imposing the capital punishment of dismissal from service without any prior show cause 
notice is against the settled Law and contrary to the principles of natural justice. Further, extremely harsh punishment 
of dismissal from service is highly excessive and shockingly disproportionate and it amounts to economic death of the 


542 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA : MARCH |4, 2026/PHALGUNA 23, 947 [PART II—SEc. 3(ii)] 


petitioner. 


2(d). Ever since his unjust dismissal from service, the petitioner could not secure any other alternative job & remained 
unemployed. He lost lively hood and incurred huge debts for his medical and domestic expenses. He is facing lot of 
hard ship and misery to eke out lively hood for all his family members. This Court has got every jurisdiction to try the 
case U/Sec.2-(A) (2) of I.D. Act, as per the settled law declared by the Hon’ble High Court. Due to domestic and 
financial problems, the petitioner could not approach this Hon’ble Court earlier; and the delay if any in filing this case 
may please be condoned by this Hon’ble Court. Therefore, he prays to set aside the dismissal order issued by the

0. Here, on the point of territorial jurisdiction of this Tribunal, it is settled Law that as per the Division Bench 
Judgment of the Hon’ble High Court reported in 997 (III) LLJ (Supp.) Il, Between: U.Chinnappa Vs. Cotton 
Corporation of India, this Tribunal has got every jurisdiction to entertain the Industrial Dispute raised by the 
petitioner/workman who was an employee of Singareni Collieries Company Ltd., Even though, the Central Govt. is 
appropriate Govt., for the respondents’-Company, the petitioner need not compulsorily raise the Industrial Dispute 
before the Central Govt. Industrial Tribunal, Hyderabad, as contended by the respondents’ company; and he can file 
this I.D. case before this Tribunal as well. Hence, the contentions of the respondents’-company on the point of 
jurisdiction of this Tribunal are not sustainable under Law. 


0(a). Further, with regard to the contention of delay and barred by limitation, this Tribunal relied on a D.B. Judgment 
of the Hon’ble Supreme Court in Civil Appeal No.257/999, dt.08.04.999 between Ajaib singh vs. Sirhind Co-op. 
Marketing-cum-Processing Service Society Ltd., & another, wherein their lordships held that:- 


“Article /37 of schedule of Limitation Act not applicable to the proceedings under ID. Act. The object of 
Industrial Disputes Act was to give succor to weaker sections of the society. The emergence of the concept of Welfare 
State implies an end to exploitation of workman and as a corollary to that collective bargaining came into it own. The 

Legislature had intended to protect workmen against victimization and exploitation by the employer and to ensure 
termination of Industrial Disputes in a peaceful manner. 


The object of the Act, therefore, is to give succor to weaker sections of the society which is a pre-requisite for 
Welfare State. To ensure industrial peace and pre-empt industrial tension, the Act further aims at enhancing the 
industrial production which is acknowledged to be life-blood of a developing society. 


The Act provides a machinery for investigation and settlement of industrial dispute ignoring the legal technicalities 
with a view to avoid delays, by specially authorized Courts which are not supposed to deny the relief on account of the 
procedural wrangles”. 


l0(b). Further, relied on a decision of the Hon’ble High Court reported in 20l2 (l) ALD 220 (DB), wherein their 
lordships held that:- 


“The Industrial Disputes Act, /947 is a social welfare legislation, which required to be interpreted keeping in 
view the goals set out in the Preamble and Directive principles of State Policy in Part-IV of the Constitution. Merely 
because workman approached to Labour Court with delay, relief cannot be denied. No indication in the Act that delay 
extinguishes right conferred on the workmen under Industrial Law. The Labour Court is conferred with very wide

discretion 9/$९०८.77-4 from considering the delay on part of workmen in granting relief. 


Section 2-4 (2) or Section 700) of the Act do not prescribe any period of limitation for raising industrial 
dispute. Articles 737 of the Limitation Act, /963 has no application (Ajaib Singh’s case supra). Merely because the 
workmen approached the Industrial Court with delay, the relief cannot be denied. The Act nowhere gives an

conferred with very wide discretion 9/83०2०7/-4 of the Act, is not precluded from considering the delay on the part of

Between: Dharampur Nagarpalika Vs. Mahendrasinh Narsinh Padhiyar their Lordship have observed that:- 


(a) Law of limitation does not apply to the proceedings under the Industrial Disputes Act, /947. 


(b) The words ‘at any time' used in Section 79 would support that there is no period of limitation in making an

(c) At the same time, the appropriate Government has to keep in mind as to whether the dispute is still existing 
or live dispute and has not become a stale claim and if that is so, the reference can be refused.

and there cannot be any hard and fast rule regarding the time for making the order of reference. 


Their Lordships have further held that: This Court shall need to regard, of course, the later decision which

...Law can be summarized that there is no prescribed time limit for the appropriate Government to exercise 
its powers under Section 79 of the Act. It is more so in view of the language used, namely, if any industrial

548 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA : MARCH |4, 2026/PHALGUNA 23, 947 [PART II—SEc. 3(ii)] 


industrial production which is acknowledged to be life-blood of a developing society. The Act provides a machinery 
for investigation and settlement of industrial dispute ignoring the legal technicalities with a view to avoid delays, by 
specially authorized Courts which are not supposed to deny the relief on account of the procedural wrangles”. 


l6(a). Further, in a decision of the Hon’ble High Court reported in 20!2 (.) ALD 220 (DB), wherein their lordships 
observed that:- 


“The Industrial Disputes Act, /947 is a social welfare legislation, which required to be interpreted keeping 
in view the goals set out in the Preamble and Directive principles of State Policy in Part-IV of the Constitution. 
The Labour Court/Industrial Tribunal is conferred with very wide discretion 9/8९८77-4 of the Act for granting 
appropriate relief”. 


7. Here, their Lordships of the Hon’ble Gujarat High Court in a case rendered on 04.05.994, Between: Management 
of Glaxo India Ltd., Vs. State of Assam and 3 others categorically observed that “a Labour Court is required to settle 
a dispute according to the principles of natural justice, equity and good conscience and law without attaching 
undue importance to legal technicalities”. 
8. Further, it is well settled law that if the Industrial Tribunal/ Labour Court is satisfied that the punishment imposed 
on the petitioner/workman is not justified, the Industrial Tribunal/ Labour Court is clothed with the power to 
reappraise the evidence in the domestic enquiry and satisfy itself whether the said evidence relied on by the Enquiry 
Officer or Respondents/ Management established the misconduct alleged against the workman. Further, $०९८.77-4 
comes into effect only at the time when the Industrial Tribunal/Labour Court consider about the punishment to be 
imposed. While previously the Industrial Tribunal/Labour Court had no power to interfere with the punishment, it is 
now clothed with such a power. Apart from the above, Industrial Tribunal/Labour Court should temper justice with 
mercy and not flog the petitioner/workman to asset our might. The power of ocean does not lie in its tumultuous tides 
but in its meditative vastness”. My above view is fortified with the observation of their Lordships of Hon’ble Madras 
High Court in a case Between: High Court of Madras Vs. R.D.Santhana Krishnan बॉ. 247 December, 2024. 
9. Here, it is to be noted that the concept of Industrial Dispute is quite broad and with the passage of time its horizon 
is being expanded. Further, the disputes are required to be resolved for the purpose of establishing peaceful and 
cordial atmosphere in an industry. Peace and harmony are the quintessential aspects which are to be kept in view 
while dealing with the “/is” or “controversy” relating to any industry. Apart from the above, whether the impugned 
punishment is so disproportionate as to shock the conscience of the Court, has to be decided on the facts of each case, 
having due regard to the gravity of misconduct & nature of duties discharged by the delinquent employee. 
20. Here, it is pertinent to note that the term “misconduct” is the intentional doing of something which the doer knows 
to be wrong, or which he does recklessly, not caring what the result may be. It includes negligence or want of proper 
care which an employee is to take. But, it is a fact that “to err is human” and “to forgive is divine”. Keeping the said 
spirit into consideration and in the interest of cause of justice, every errant conduct of an employee of an organization 
could not be treated as grave misconduct. Further, it is settled law that promoting empathy and understanding by 
encouraging forgiveness, which is a divine quality transcending human limitation, should be preferred to anything else 
in the given circumstances. My above view is fortified by observation of their Lordships of the Hon’ble Supreme 
Court in a judgment rendered Between: Ratilal Jhaverbhai Parmar Vs State Of Gujarat 4.27 October, 2024. 
2. Further, the Hon’ble Madras High Court observed in a case rendered in Management of Hyudai Motor India Ltd 
Vs. T.Sudhakar ... on 377 January, 2022: 
“When scales of justice stands balanced in a given case, the tilt to be exercised should be in favour 

of the poor workmen rather than the mighty Managements.” 
22. Here, I am of the opinion that for promoting ethical behavior and integrity for Public Servants, the Latin Maxim 
(Memento Mori: remember that you must die”) acts as a check against selfish to selfless service. It serves as a 
reminder that: “when office is gone, only the legacy of their character remains”. So, the old Adam or old Man or old- 
self of him or her must die. Otherwise, it will kill them. In summary, Memento Mori serves as a Sobering, yet 
empowering reminder that allows Public Servants to focus on leaving a positive, lasting impact rather than chasing, 
selfish and temporary goals. 
23. Therefore, by taking a holistic view of the matter, I am of the considered view that the extreme punishment of 
removal imposed by the respondents/corporation against the petitioner/workman is harsh, disproportionate and shocks 
to conscience of this Tribunal, hence, deserves to be modified since the disciplinary authority cannot be permitted to 
act arbitrarily and work like a Roman Knight and it cannot be allowed a fight between David and Goliath as in the 
present case on hand. Moreover, facts of this case attracts the proverbial saying “Every saint has a past and every 
sinner has a future” and Biblical proverbs “Speak up for those who cannot speak for themselves, for the rights of all 
who are destitute” and “Speak up and judge fairly; defend the rights of the poor and needy.” Further, “Heavens 
would not have fallen if one more opportunity is given for the petitioner”. 
24. This Tribunal has perused, analyzed and meditated upon the case at hand, the case laws and principles of law 
referred above. In view of the above facts and circumstances and keeping in view of the principle “temper justice with 
mercy” and to meet the ends of justice, this Tribunal is of the opinion that the punishment of dismissal from service 
imposed on the petitioner/workman is disproportionate and shocks the conscience of this Tribunal and hence, it 
deserves to be modified appropriately. It appears from the record that the petitioner rendered short service in the

respondents’ company and he is out of employment ever since his dismissal from service in 20l9. Hence, this 
Tribunal is of the considered view that that the petitioner/workman deserves to be reinstated into service as “AFRESH 
BADLI WORKER” only. Consequently, he is not entitled to any back wages, any continuity of service and any other 
attendant benefits. Hence, the punishment of dismissal from service imposed by the Respondents’ Company is hereby 
modified. Accordingly, the Points 2 & 3 are answered.

into service as “AFRESH BADLI WORKER?” only and he is not entitled to any back wages, any continuity of service 
and any other attendant benefits. However, the petitioner is entitled to salary only from the date of publication of the 
Award. Copy of the Award be sent to the appropriate Government for publication. Both parties shall bear their own

4. Now the question is whether the punishment of removal from service is disproportionate or not? 


4(a). It is settled law that the object of I.D.Act is to give succor to weaker sections of the society and it is a social 
welfare legislation. Here, there is no “Plumbline Precision” for deciding the proportionality of punishment, which 
depends upon the facts and circumstances of each case. The Industrial Tribunal/Labour Court is empowered to 
exercise discretionary powers U/Sec.ll-A of Industrial Disputes Act for judicious adjudication of the industrial 
disputes. Several factors like nature of duty, past service past conduct, previous penalties if any and the discipline 
required to maintain in the department, victimization and plea of the petitioner/workman and the punishment must be

l6. Here, this Tribunal relied on a Division Bench Judgment of the Hon’ble Supreme Court rendered in Civil Appeal

“The object of Industrial Disputes Act was to give succor to weaker sections of the society. The emergence of the 
concept of Welfare State implies an end to exploitation of workman and as a corollary to that collective bargaining 
came into it own. The Legislature had intended to protect workmen against victimization and exploitation by the 
employer and to ensure termination of Industrial Disputes in a peaceful manner. 


“The object of the Act, therefore, is to give succor to weaker sections of the society which is a pre-requisite for 
Welfare State. To ensure industrial peace and pre-empt industrial tension, the Act further aims at enhancing the 
industrial production which is acknowledged to be life-blood of a developing society. The Act provides a machinery 
for investigation and settlement of industrial dispute ignoring the legal technicalities with a view to avoid delays, by 
specially authorized Courts which are not supposed to deny the relief on account of the procedural wrangles ”’. 


6(a). Further, in a decision of the Hon’ble High Court reported in 20I2 (l) ALD 220 (DB), wherein their lordships 
observed that:- 


“The Industrial Disputes Act, /947 is a social welfare legislation, which required to be interpreted keeping 
in view the goals set out in the Preamble and Directive principles of State Policy in Part-IV of the Constitution. 
The Labour Court/Industrial Tribunal is conferred with very wide discretion ७/8९८,/7-4 of the Act for granting 
appropriate relief”.

of Glaxo India Ltd., Vs. State of Assam and 3 others categorically observed that “a Labour Court is required to settle

8. Further, it is well settled law that if the Industrial Tribunal/ Labour Court is satisfied that the punishment imposed 
on the petitioner/workman is not justified, the Industrial Tribunal/Labour Court is clothed with the power to 
reappraise the evidence in the domestic enquiry and satisfy itself whether the said evidence relied on by the Enquiry 
Officer or Respondents/ Management established the misconduct alleged against the workman. Further, $९८.7/-१ 
comes into effect only at the time when the Industrial Tribunal/Labour Court consider about the punishment to be 
imposed. While previously the Industrial Tribunal/Labour Court had no power to interfere with the punishment, it is 
now clothed with such a power. Apart from the above, Industrial Tribunal/Labour Court should temper justice with 
mercy and not flog the petitioner/workman to asset our might. The power of ocean does not lie in its tumultuous tides 
but in its meditative vastness”. My above view is fortified with the observation of their Lordships of Hon’ble Madras 
High Court in a case Between: High Court of Madras Vs. R.D.Santhana Krishnan बॉ. 2477 December, 2024. 


9. Here, it is to be noted that the concept of Industrial Dispute is quite broad and with the passage of time its horizon 
is being expanded. Further, the disputes are required to be resolved for the purpose of establishing peaceful and 
cordial atmosphere in an industry. Peace and harmony are the quintessential aspects which are to be kept in view 
while dealing with the “/is” or “controversy” relating to any industry. Apart from the above, whether the impugned 
punishment is so disproportionate as to shock the conscience of the Court, has to be decided on the facts of each case, 
having due regard to the gravity of misconduct & nature of duties discharged by the delinquent employee. 


20. Here, it is pertinent to note that the term “misconduct” is the intentional doing of something which the doer knows 
to be wrong, or which he does recklessly, not caring what the result may be. It includes negligence or want of proper 
care which an employee is to take. But, it is a fact that “to err is human” and “to forgive is divine”. Keeping the said 
spirit into consideration and in the interest of cause of justice, every errant conduct of an employee of an organization 
could not be treated as grave misconduct. Further, it is settled law that promoting empathy and understanding by 
encouraging forgiveness, which is a divine quality transcending human limitation, should be preferred to anything else 
in the given circumstances. My above view is fortified by observation of their Lordships of the Hon’ble Supreme 
Court in a judgment rendered Between: Ratilal Jhaverbhai Parmar Vs State Of Gujarat 4.27 October, 2024. 


2. Further, the Hon’ble Madras High Court observed in a case rendered in Management of Hyudai Motor India Ltd 
Vs. T.Sudhakar ... on 377 January, 2022: 


“When scales of justice stands balanced in a given case, the tilt to be exercised should be in favour 
of the poor workmen rather than the mighty Managements.” 


22. Here, I am of the opinion that for promoting ethical behavior and integrity for Public Servants, the Latin Maxim 
(Memento Mori: remember that you must die”) acts as a check against selfish to selfless service. It serves as a 
reminder that: “when office is gone, only the legacy of their character remains”. So, the old Adam or old Man or old- 
self of him or her must die. Otherwise, it will kill them. In summary, Memento Mori serves as a Sobering, yet 
empowering reminder that allows Public Servants to focus on leaving a positive, lasting impact rather than chasing, 
selfish and temporary goals. 


23. Therefore, by taking a holistic view of the matter, I am of the considered view that the extreme punishment of 
removal imposed by the respondents/corporation against the petitioner/workman is harsh, disproportionate and shocks 
to conscience of this Tribunal, hence, deserves to be modified since the disciplinary authority cannot be permitted to 
act arbitrarily and work like a Roman Knight and it cannot be allowed a fight between David and Goliath as in the 
present case on hand. Moreover, facts of this case attracts the proverbial saying “Every saint has a past and every 
sinner has a future” and Biblical proverbs “Speak up for those who cannot speak for themselves, for the rights of all 
who are destitute” and “Speak up and judge fairly; defend the rights of the poor and needy.” Further, “Heavens 
would not have fallen if one more opportunity is given for the petitioner”. 


24. This Tribunal has perused, analyzed and meditated upon the case at hand, the case laws and principles of law 
referred above. In view of the above facts and circumstances and keeping in view of the principle “temper justice with 
mercy” and to meet the ends of justice, this Tribunal is of the opinion that the punishment of removal from service 
imposed on the petitioner is disproportionate and shocks the conscience of this Tribunal and hence, it deserves to be 
modified appropriately. It appears from the record that the petitioner rendered service of 8-years only in the 
respondents’ company and he is out of employment ever since his dismissal from service. Hence, this Tribunal is of

stern disciplinary action against him. Hence, the punishment of dismissal from service imposed by the Respondents’

The above named workman being represented by President, Koyala Mazdoor Congress raised an Industrial 
Dispute before the Dy. CLC(C), Asansol through Samadhan portal dated 0.0.2023. The contention of the union is 
that Manoj Kumar Pati, a General Mazdoor bearing U.M. No.l02066 was posted at Madhusudanpur Colliery, Kajora 
Area. By order dated 09.08.203, Manoj Kumar Pati was deployed to perform the duty of attendance clerk at 
Madhusudanpur Colliery but after rendering continuous service for a long period, the management of ECL refused to 
regularize his service as attendance clerk. A conciliation proceeding was held which resulted in failure. The 
Government of India through the Office of the Deputy Chief Labour Commissioner (Central), Asansol issued Order 
No. (0)/2023/E. dated 22.05.2023 whereby in exercise of powers conferred by clause (d) of sub-section () and sub- 
section (2A) of Section 0 of the Industrial Disputes Act, 947 (/4 of 947) referred the scheduled dispute for 
adjudication by this Tribunal. 


“ Whether the action of the management of Madhusudanpur Colliery, Kajora Area, M/s. ECL in not paying 
the amount of differencial wages and not regularisation to the post of Attendance Clerk to Sri Manoj Kumar 
Pati is justified or no ? If not, what relief the workman is entitled to”. 


l. On receiving Order No. (40)/2023/E. dated 22.05.2023 from the Office of the Deputy Chief Labour 
Commissioner (Central), Asansol, Ministry of Labour, Government of India, for adjudication of the dispute a 
Reference case was registered on 30.05.2023 and an order was passed for issuing notice to the parties through 
registered post, directing them to appear and submit their written statements along with relevant documents in support 
of their claims. 


2; Manoj Kumar Pati filed written statement on !3.09.2023 through Koyala Mazdoor Congress. The facts which 
unfolded from the written statement is that Manoj Kumar Pati, a permanent employee of ECL was posted as General

Mazdoor. Subsequently he was deployed as attendance clerk against permanent vacancy for managing attendance of 
the employees at Madhusudanpur Colliery. He performed his duty continuously till initiating this Industrial Dispute. It 
is contended that the workman requested the management to pay him difference of wage of Clerk Grade-II and the 
amount which was being paid to him as a General Mazdoor in Cat-I. The aggrieved workman also requested the 
management for regularizing him in the post of Clerk but the management of ECL did not consider his request. 
Further case of union is that according to the Memorandum of Settlement dated 02.08.203, Manoj Kumar Pati was 
deployed as attendance clerk but the management did not pay him the wages of Clerical Grade-lII. It is asserted that 
the management regularized number of workers as Clerk without any test or examination. It is submitted that 
Ramakant Yadav, Sudip Mitra, Bhakta Das Badyakar, Ramawadh Bouri of the same colliery were regularized as clerk 
without undergoing any test or examination. Accordingly, Manoj Kumar Pati, who performs service in the capacity of 
clerk for ten years without any promotion should be regularized to the post of clerk as per the provision of Certified 
Standing Order of the company, which lays down that if a worker performed any particular job continuously for a 
period of three months or above, he should be regularized to that post. It is further ascertained that management of 
Madhusudanpur Colliery have the requirement of attendance clerk and Manoj Kumar Pati fulfills all the requirements 
for the post of clerk, as such he should be regularized to that post and should be paid difference of wages from the 
date of his working as a clerk. 


3. Management of ECL contested the case by filing written statement on !3.09.2023. The version of the 
management is that the post of attendance clerk comes under Clerical Grade as it is a centralized post. Selection to 
clerical post is done by the ECL Headquarters and for this purpose notifications are issued from time to time for filling 
vacancy in the post. Candidates having requisite qualification are required to apply for this post and they are selected 
for clerical posts only after they qualify in the selection test conducted by the management. Therefore, the workman is 
not entitled to be regularized to the post of clerk unless he fulfills certain criteria. It is admitted by the management 
that the Manoj Kumar Pati has been placed to manage attendance work at colliery Pit No. 7 vide Office Order No. 
MSP/6/689 dated 09.08.20I3. It is further stated that in case of encadrement/regularization of a workman from 
General Mazdoor Cat-I to Clerk Grade-III, no incremental benefit is given if the prevailing basic of the General 
Mazdoor is more than the minimum basic of Clerk Grade-III. If the prevailing basic of the concerned workman is less 
than the minimum basic of Clerk Grade-III, then the workman is given the benefit by fixing his pay at minimum basic 
of Clerk Grade-III. Displaying a chart, showing comparative basic pay of Manoj Kumar Pati and the minimum 
monthly basic of Clerk Grade-III from the year 20l3 to 2023, Management claimed that basic pay of Manoj Kumar 
Pati since 20l3 was already more than the minimum basic pay of Clerk Grade — III. As such no difference of wage is 
payable to the workman and the workman is not entitled to any outstanding dues. It is urged that Manoj Kumar Pati 
was never regularized to the post of Clerk Grade -III and he is not entitled to any benefit claimed. 


4. The central point for consideration is whether Manoj Kumar Pati, a General Mazdoor, deployed as 
attendance Clerk should be regularized to the said post and whether he is entitled to payment of any difference of 
wages. 


5. Union examined Manoj Kumar Pati as WW-l. He filed an affidavit-in-chief and claimed that in a 
Memorandum of Settlement dated 02.08.20l3, management agreed to place him as attendance clerk along with other 
workman and Office Order No. MSP/6/689 dated 09.08.20I3 was issued. The witness further averred that the 
management received the benefit of service rendered by him for several years but did not place him in Clerk Grade-II 
and did not pay him difference of wages between General Mazdoor and Clerk Grade-II. The workman claimed that he 
completed one year of service as attendance clerk on 0.09.204 and should be paid the wage of Clerk Grade-II w.e.f. 
0.09.204. In respect of the comparative chart showing statement of wages from 20l3 to August 2023, the workman 
claimed that he had been performing the job of Clerk Grade-II and the basic pay of Clerk Grade-II should have been 
taken into consideration instead of Clerk Grade-III. The workman witness further stated that the management of 
Kajora Area as well as other areas of ECL had sent the names of other employees of ECL for regularization who were 
deployed to work in clerical jobs and the competent authority of ECL approved the proposal of their regularization. It 
is urged that the regularization process should also be considered with consistency but the management adopted pick 
and choose policy according to their wish, ignoring legitimate claims.

It appears from his examination in chief that Manoj Kumar Pati was initially appointed at Kalidaspur Colliery, ECL 
and he came on transfer to Madhusudanpur Colliery in 2004. After he was placed as attendance clerk on the basis of a 
settlement dated 02.08.20I3 (Exhibit W-3), the workman submitted an application dated 9.05.20!7 before Personnel 
Manager for his regularization to the post of attendance clerk (Exhibit W-4). He submitted another application for his 
regularization as attendance clerk (Exhibit W-5). He produced a copy of Office Order dated 2.0!.20l! whereby 
similarly placed workers were regularized in their respective posts where they were deputed to work. Copy of Office 
Order dated 2.0i.20l! has been produced as Exhibit W-6. The workman produced a copy of Memorandum of 
Settlement where the management agreed to pay difference of wages on regularization (Exhibit W-8). Thereafter, a 
proposal dated 06.05.209 was initiated at the Colliery level regarding regularization of Manoj Kumar Pati to the post 
of attendance clerk (Exhibit W-9). The workman claimed that at present he receives a daily wage of Rs. 27I3.5] per 
day but could not state the difference of wages he would be entitled to if regularized. In cross-examination, the 
witness denied that in all cases before posting in clerical grade, a selection procedure has to be carried out. Workman 
denied that for regularization in clerical grade, the preconditions which have to be fulfilled are educational criteria and 
participation in the selection process. Witness deposed that in many cases, persons have been posted in clerical cadre 
without any selection test. It transpires from his testimony that he was not aware about the notifications of 05.06.204, 
.02.206 and 02.02.208 issued by the management for holding written examination for the post of Clerical Grade- 
III. The witness was unable to state if other employees of the establishment applied for the post of clerical grade. The 
witness admitted that if his basic pay was computed on the basis of daily wage @ Rs. 273.5 for twenty six days, his 
basic pay would be more than starting pay in the post of attendance clerk. 


6. Mr. Proloy Dasgupta, management witness filed an affidavit-in-chief admitting the factual aspects. The 
witness has clearly stated in paragraph 4 of the affidavit that the post of attendance clerk is a centralized post and 
selection to clerical grade is carried out by ECL Headquarters. It is stated that notifications are issued from time to 
time according to vacancy in the post and candidates having requisite qualification apply for the post and their 
selection to the post of clerical grade is considered only after qualifying in the selection test. The aggrieved workman 
not having fulfilled such requirements do not qualify to be regularized to the post of clerk. The witness stated that in 
case of regularization from General Mazdoor Cat-I to Clerk Grade-III, no incremental benefit is given if the basic of 
the concerned workman aspiring for the post in Clerk Grade has a higher minimum pay than the basic pay of Clerk 
Grade-I. The witness further deposed that since 20l3, Manoj Kumar Pati was already receiving more than the 
minimum basic of Clerk Grade-II, he is not entitled to any difference of wage or any outstanding dues.

During cross-examination, the management witness deposed that Ramakant Yadav and Ramawadh Bouri were 
regularized as Store Clerk Grade-III from their earlier post of Clerk Grade-III on the basis of recommendation of 
Departmental Promotion Committee. It transpires from further cross-examination of MW-| that the aforesaid persons 
did not apply in response to any notification and their selection was not through any test. So far as circulation of 
notification is concerned, the witness stated that it was displayed on the Notice Board and no separate notice were 
issued to eligible candidates. It may be gathered from the cross-examination of management witness that Manoj 
Kumar Pati is functioning as attendance clerk from the year 20l3 without interruption. The witness also admitted that 
Manoj Kumar Pati is matriculate and he served for more than three years in the post of attendance clerk. The witness 
admitted that apart from holding test there is process for selection by fulfillment of educational qualification as well as 
length of service of candidate and he is also required to undergo an examination held by the management. The witness 
deposed that Ramakant Yadav and Ramawadh Bouri were regularized to Clerk Grade-III in the year 20l] on the 
recommendation of departmental promotion committee/selection committee of ECL headquarters but the witness was 
unable to state if any test was held for their regularization to the post of Clerk Grade-III. A suggestion was put to 
management witness by the union representative that Ramakant Yadav and Ramawadh Bouri were regularized to the 
post of Clerk Grade-III without any examination or appearing in a test which the witness denied. No specific 
document was thereafter produced by the management to establish that examination was held for regularization of the 
two workmen in clerical grade. 


de Mr. Rakesh Kumar, union representative argued that Manoj Kumar Pati was placed as attendance clerk on 
the basis of a Memorandum of Settlement. He performed satisfactorily in the said capacity for several years, since 
August 203 but the management of ECL did not considered his application for regularization to the post and no 
difference of pay has been granted in favour of the workman for the duties performed by him. It is argued that Manoj 
Kumar Pati is a matriculate. It is argued by the union representative that several other workmen from other Collieries 
have been deployed and then regularized as Clerk without undergoing any selection process or any examination. In 
the instant case, the workman has been functioning against a vacant post and the management should regularize him in 
the said post and paid his dues towards difference of pay for the work done by him as attendance clerk. 


8. P.K. Das, learned advocate for the management strenuously argued that initially the workman was placed at 
Pit No. 7 of Madhusudanpur Colliery to manage the attendance work w.e.f. 09.08.20I3 on the basis of Memorandum 
of Settlement but he was never posted as a clerk and he is not entitled to the benefit of being regularized or being 
granted the difference of pay between the post of Clerk Grade-III and General Mazdoor unless he applied against a 
notification issued from time to time to fill such post. Only after appearing in the selection test and on being 
recommended by the Departmental Promotion Committee, an employee can be posted in the clerical grade. 


9, I have considered the rival arguments in the light of facts and circumstances of the case disclosed in the 
pleadings and evidence adduced by both parties. It is abundantly clear that Manoj Kumar Pati who was initially posted 
as a General Mazdoor on 09.0.2004 (Exhibit W-), was deployed to function as an attendance clerk from 09.08.203, 
on the basis of an Office Order produced as Exhibit W-2. It appears from the record that Memorandum of Settlement 
under section!2(3) of Industrial Disputes Act, 947 was executed on 02.08.20I3 by representatives of the union and 
the management wherein it was agreed before the Assistant Labour Commissioner (Central), Raniganj that Manoj 
Kumar Pati would be placed to manage attendance work at Madhusudanpur Colliery. Copy of Form ‘H’ has been 
produced as Exhibit W-3. Though Manoj Kumar Pati claimed that he was placed as attendance clerk, both the 
Memorandum of Settlement dated 02.08.20l3 and Office Order dated 09.08.20I3 disclose that he was placed to 
manage the attendance work at Madhusudanpur Colliery and certainly it was not any placement order as attendance 
clerk. The workman has been continuously rendered service in the capacity of attendance clerk since 09.08.203. The 
concerned workman made several representations before the Manager (Personnel) and Agent, Madhusudanpur 
Colliery seeking his regularization to the post of attendance clerk. Copies of applications dated 9.05.20I7 and 
3.09.202] have been produced as Exhibit W-4 and W-5 respectively. On 06.05.20l9, a proposal was made for 
regularization/encadrement of two employees namely Manoj Kumar Pati and Subhas Sahana, Switch Board attendant 
to the post of Clerk Grade-III. A copy of the proposal signed by the Deputy Manager (Personnel) has been produced 
by the union as Exhibit W-9. From the aforesaid documents, it is affirmed that the management of ECL was fully 
conscious that Manoj Kumar Pati is functioning as Clerk Grade-III and that he proposed for his regularization. 
Workman has produced copy of Office Order dated 2.0.20I at Exhibit W-6 which reveals that on recommendation 
of Departmental Promotion Committee constituted at the headquarter level, the competent authority upon 
recommendation of Departmental Promotion/Selection Committee constituted at headquarter level regularized 
Ramakant Yadav and Ramawadh Bouri as Clerk Grade-III. The management witness in his cross examination dated 
06..2024 deposed that Ramakant Yadav and Ramawadh Bouri Clerk Grade-III were regularized as Clerk Grade-III 
on recommendation of Departmental Promotion Committee and further stated that their selection was not based on 
any test. It is therefore manifestly clear that management of ECL while regularizing some of its employees to the post 
of clerical cadre did not issue any prior notification and the concerned persons without applying against any 
notification and without appearing in any examination were recommended to fill up clerical posts. 


0. Mr. Das has produced copies of notification dated 05.06.20I4, .02.20l6 and 02.02.20l8 which are 


[भाग W—davs 3()] भारत का राजपत्र : मार्च 4, 2026/फाल्गुन 23, 947 57] 


notifications for the written examination for selection to Clerk Grade-III from eligible departmental candidates. Manoj 
Kumar Pati in his evidence stated that he was not informed about such circulars. According to the management, if a 
person from a lower cadre is placed to function as a clerk, he would not be entitled to any difference of pay if the basic 
pay of the person so deployed is more than the minimum basic pay of Clerk Grade-III. It has been argued that Manoj 
Kumar Pati was receiving higher pay than the minimum pay of Clerk Grade-III. Therefore, he is not entitled to get 
difference of pay. In the instant case, the aggrieved workman has rendered continuous service as attendance clerk for 
ten years without being regularized to the post. The management has relied upon a scheme for Ministerial Staff in the 
general Clerical Cadre which has been circulated vide II No. 34 dated 7.07.984. For the purpose of being designated 
as Clerk Grade-III, the required minimum qualification is matriculation or any equivalent examination from any 
recognized Board of Examination and he would be eligible for promotion to the post of Clerk Grade-II by the 
recommendation of Departmental Promotion Committee. In the instant case, it would appear from the written 
statement and affidavit-in-chief of management witness that in the year 20l3, Manoj Kumar Pati was receiving a 
higher basic pay as General Mazdoor than the minimum basic pay of Clerk Grade-III. Since 09.08.203, the workman 
has rendered continuously served as attendance clerk of Madhusudanpur Colliery. Admittedly, the aggrieved 
workman is a matriculate. ॥५४-] in his cross-examination has admitted that Manoj Kumar Pati is a matriculate and he 
has served for more than three years as attendance clerk. By dint of such educational qualification and experience he 
is already receiving a basic pay higher that Clerk Grade-III. Manoj Kumar Pati is found eligible for his regularization 
to the post of Clerk Grade-II immediately on completion of three years in the clerical post. Therefore, he is entitled to 
be regularized to the post Clerk Grade-II w.e.f. 09.08.20I6. There is preponderance of evidence to prove that 
regularization of subordinate staff members to clerical grade of the management were considered on the basis of their 
educational qualification and experience without holding any examination or separate selection process. The case of 
Ramakant Jadhav and Ram Awadh Bouri clearly indicate that they were regularized to the post of Clerk Grade-II 
without any selecting procedure. The management should certainly strive to bring about a parity in treatment of its 
employees. I therefore hold that Manoj Kumar Pati is entitled to be regularized to the post of Clerk Grade-II and is 
entitled to difference of wage between Clerk Grade-II and pay received by him w.e.f. 09.08.20l6 and disburse the 
dues in respect of the difference of pay in the post of Clerk Grade-II w.e.f. 09.08.206 within a period of three months 
from communication of this order. 


Hence, 
ORDERED 


The Industrial Dispute is allowed in part against the management of ECL. Manoj Kumar Pati be regularized 
to the post of Clerk Grade-II w.e.f. 09.08.206 and he shall also be entitled to receive difference of pay for the post of 
Clerk Grade-II w.e.f. 09.08.206. Management of ECL shall complete the entire procedure within three months of 
communication of this order. Let copies of the Award in duplicate be sent to the Ministry of Labour, Government of 
India, New Delhi for information and Notification.

In exercise of powers conferred under clause (d) of Sub-section (l) and Sub-section (2A) of Section 0 of the 
Industrial Disputes Act, !947 (4 of 947), the Government of India through the Ministry of Labour, vide its Order 
No. L-2202/76/2022-IR(CM-II) dated 03.08.2022 has been pleased to refer the following dispute between the

“Whether the demand of the President, Koyala Mazdoor Congress (HMS), Asansol in his letter dated 
26/6/2027 (copy enclosed) to reinstate in service to Sri Rabila! Majhi. U.G. Loader, who was dismissed vide letter 
No. KA:PM:C-6:0:3369/24 dated 2/0०7//9965(८०779 enclosed) against the action of the management of Khas Kajora 
Colliery, Kajora Area, M/s E.C.Ltd. in their letter No. KKC/P&IR/C-6/Re-State/33l dated 72/26/2077 (copy 
enclosed), is proper, legal and justified? If yes, what relief the workman concerned is entitled to? ” 


l. On receiving Order No. L-2202/76/2022-IR(CM-II) dated 03.08.2022 from the Government of India, 
Ministry of Labour, New Delhi for adjudication of the dispute, a Reference case was registered on 0.08.2022 and an 
order was passed for issuing notice to the parties through registered post, directing them to appear and submit their 
written statements along with relevant documents in support of their claims. 


2, Rabilal Majhi, the dismissed workman filed written statement in this case on 27.03.2023 through
